29.text: This lab is about wasted inference work, so even the imports hint at the story: same model, but now we can time the naive path against the cached one.

30.text: Same dataset, same task. That keeps the focus on the inference optimization rather than on model or data changes.

31.text: Randomness is only supporting cast here; the real experiment is how much repeated computation we can eliminate during generation.

32.text: Timing matters in this lab because KV cache is not a theoretical nicety, it is the optimization that makes autoregressive decoding practical.

34.text: PyTorch gives us the same baseline model as before. The important difference is that attention can now remember yesterday's K and V instead of recomputing them.

35.text: Nothing dramatic changes in the layer stack. That is the point: the speedup comes from preserving history, not from inventing a new model.

36.text: Softmax and loss stay ordinary. What changes is how much of the prefix attention has to rebuild at each decoding step.

38.text: Benchmarks only mean something if the runs are comparable, so we lock the stochastic pieces down before measuring.

96.text: Forward now takes an optional kv_cache, this is the entire innovation of this lab.

98.text: Project queries for the new positions only. During cached inference, this is a single token.

99.text: Project keys for the new positions only.

100.text: Project values for the new positions only.

102.text: If we have a cache from previous steps, prepend it.

103.text: Unpack the cached K and V tensors from previous positions.

104.text: This is the crucial reuse step: old keys stay alive, and only the new key is appended. The history grows without being recomputed.

105.text: Values follow the same pattern as keys, completing the cached prefix. The new token now sees the full past through reused K/V rather than rebuilt K/V.

107.text: Save the updated cache for the next step, it grows by one position each time.

108.text: T_total = total sequence length including cached positions.

110.text: Attention: Q is (B, heads, T_new, hd), K is (B, heads, T_total, hd). The result is (B, heads, T_new, T_total).

112.text: Build the causal mask with torch.triu: each new query at absolute position T_total-T_new+i can attend to all positions up to and including itself, but not beyond.

113.text: Replace scores for future positions with negative infinity. After softmax, these become exactly zero, enforcing the causal constraint that tokens cannot peek ahead.

116.text: Weighted sum of values and reshape.

117.text: Return both the output AND the updated cache, the cache is passed to the next step.

120.text: The two-layer feed-forward network, unchanged from previous labs. The MLP operates per-position and does not need any caching since it has no cross-position state.

123.text: Project each token's representation into a 4x wider hidden space for richer computation.

124.text: Compress the expanded hidden representation back down to the original embedding dimension.

126.text: Run the input through the two-layer feed-forward network with ReLU activation.

127.text: Two linear layers with ReLU in between. The expansion to 4x width gives the network more room to learn nonlinear transformations before compressing back down.

130.text: Transformer block, now threads the KV cache through.

133.text: Normalize activations before the attention sublayer. Pre-norm keeps gradients well-behaved and is the standard in modern transformers like LLaMA.

134.text: The attention sublayer, now accepting an optional KV cache. When a cache is provided, it only processes new positions and prepends cached keys and values.

138.text: Forward now accepts and returns a cache.

139.text: Attention: receives cache, returns updated cache.

140.text: Add the attention output back to the input via a residual connection. The MLP and attention each contribute refinements without overwriting the original representation.

141.text: MLP with residual (MLP doesn't need a cache).

142.text: Return both the block's output and the updated KV cache. The caller collects caches from all layers and passes them back on the next generation step.

151.text: A stack of transformer blocks, each with its own attention and MLP. During cached inference, each layer maintains its own independent KV cache.

164.text: Combine token and position embeddings, normalize.

165.text: Collect updated caches from each layer.

167.text: Grab the cache for this layer (or None on the first pass).

168.text: Forward through the layer, receiving the updated cache.

169.text: Save this layer's updated cache into the collection. On the next generation step, it will be passed back so the layer can skip recomputing past keys and values.

176.text: Use CPU for this tiny model since it trains in seconds without a GPU.

177.text: Instantiate the model with the same architecture as lab 03. The only difference is that the forward pass now supports an optional KV cache for efficient generation.

180.text: Set up the Adam optimizer with momentum and epsilon tuned for this small model.

183.text: Training loop, caches are ignored during training (standard teacher-forced training).

194.text: Clear out any leftover gradients from the previous step so they do not accumulate.

195.text: Compute gradients for every parameter by propagating the loss backward through the graph.

196.text: Linearly reduce the learning rate from its initial value down to zero over the course of training.

197.text: Write the decayed learning rate into every parameter group so the optimizer uses it.

199.text: Apply the optimizer step, adjusting every parameter in the direction that reduces the loss.

208.text: Temperature controls the sampling distribution's sharpness. At 0.5, high-probability tokens become even more dominant, producing more conservative but coherent names.

210.text: Switch to eval mode for inference.

218.text: Naive generation: re-run the FULL sequence through the model at every step. This is O(n^3) total attention.

220.text: Track attention operations to quantify the difference.

223.text: Fixed seed per sample so naive and cached produce identical outputs.

224.text: Same seed as cached generation, outputs MUST match.

225.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token so the model starts fresh.

227.text: Feed the ENTIRE sequence so far. This is the waste, we recompute Q/K/V for all previous tokens.

228.text: Count attention operations: T*T per head, for all heads.

229.text: O(T^2) per step, and T grows each step, giving O(T^3) total.

231.text: No cache, everything is recomputed from scratch every step.

240.text: KV-cached generation: only process the NEW token each step. O(n^2) total attention.

242.text: Count the attention operations (Q times K multiply-adds) at each step so we can precisely measure how much computation the KV cache saves.

245.text: Same seed, outputs will be identical.

246.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token so the model starts fresh.

247.text: Initialize the cache as empty since no tokens have been processed yet on the first pass.

249.text: First step: no cache yet, process the full initial sequence (just BOS).

251.text: Position zero for the very first token. The positional embedding needs this offset to assign the correct position encoding to the BOS token.

253.text: Subsequent steps: only feed the LAST token. This is the key optimization, one token instead of the full sequence.

254.text: Start position = where this token sits in the sequence.

255.text: Attention ops: T_new * T_total per head. With T_new=1, this is just T_total, linear, not quadratic.

256.text: This is the entire payoff of the lab in one line: feed one fresh token in, get one larger cache out. The old prefix survives as state instead of being rebuilt from scratch.

257.text: Randomly draw one token from the probability distribution for stochastic generation.

269.text: Disable gradient tracking for both generation methods so the comparison is fair and neither wastes time computing gradients during inference.

270.text: Start the wall clock for the naive path. Read the number it produces with suspicion: at one layer and 16 dimensions the arithmetic the cache removes is smaller than Python's per-call overhead, so this timer is mostly measuring the interpreter.

271.text: Generate 20 names with no cache, recomputing the whole prefix at every step, and return the exact attention-operation count alongside the names. The count is the measurement that matters here; the stopwatch is along for the ride.

274.text: Time the cached path the same way, over the same 20 names and the same seeds. Both loops make the same number of forward calls, so the fixed overhead cancels and only the shrunken attention term is left to show up — and at this scale it does not.

280.text: Verify outputs are IDENTICAL, the cache is an optimization, not an approximation. Same model, same weights, same random seed = same output.

281.text: Side-by-side comparison of every generated name.

282.text: Flag any mismatch (there shouldn't be any).

291.text: The headline is a count of work actually performed, so it is exact and reproducible on any machine. Wall clock comes later, with caveats.

294.text: 4.3x fewer attention operations over these 20 names. An operation reduction is not a speedup: the projections, the MLP, and the Python around them are unchanged, so this bounds the win rather than reporting it.

299.text: Evaluate the closed form at T = block_size so it can be reconciled with the measured count. The two disagree, and the reason is worth a line rather than a hand-wave.

300.text: Average decode steps per name, measured rather than assumed. These names stop on BOS after about 5.8 steps, so generation never reaches position 16 and the formula's T = 16 was never the right input.

303.text: Naive: sum of t^2 for t=1..T = T(T+1)(2T+1)/6. Cubic growth.

304.text: Cached: sum of t for t=1..T = T(T+1)/2. Quadratic growth.

305.text: The ratio grows linearly with sequence length, longer sequences benefit more from caching.

306.text: Print measured against theoretical and then explain the gap, instead of quietly reporting whichever is more flattering. 4.3x versus 11.0x is not an error in either number.

308.text: Re-evaluate the same (2T+1)/3 at the observed 5.8 steps and it lands on 4.2x, right where the counter did. The saving grows with sequence length, so a corpus of six-letter names sees the very small end of it.

314.text: End-to-end wall clock, reported because the reader will want it and then immediately qualified. This ratio has been seen anywhere from below 1.00x to a few x on the same code — it moves with machine load, which is a fact about the benchmark, not about the cache.

317.text: Labelled 'NOT a speedup figure' in the output itself. Twenty six-letter names on a 16-dimensional model is a measurement of dispatch overhead with a little attention arithmetic hidden inside it.

318.text: Rather than explaining away an unhelpful number, the lab says what the number is measuring and then fixes the benchmark below. That is the more useful lesson: the optimization was fine, the experiment was wrong.

341.text: Take the fastest of N runs, not the mean. Anything else sharing the CPU can only ever make a run slower, so the mean measures the machine's mood while the minimum measures the code — which is why the table below reads as a clean trend instead of scatter.

349.text: Seed the running minimum at infinity so the first iteration always wins. Cheap, and it avoids a special case that would be easy to get subtly wrong.

353.text: One timer around one call, then keep the smallest. Loop overhead sits outside the measured region, so it cannot contaminate the number the way an outer average would.

357.text: The section that finally demonstrates the effect: measure the one thing the cache changes — a single decode step — at context lengths a serving system would actually reach.

359.text: A fresh attention module on random activations is enough, because timing depends on tensor shapes rather than on trained weights. Reusing the trained model would have tied this benchmark to block_size = 16, which is precisely the length where the effect is invisible.

361.text: T = 64, 256, 1024, 2048. Sweeping the context length is what turns a single ambiguous ratio into a curve, and a curve you can see the shape of is worth more than any one timing.

362.text: The naive input: the whole prefix, re-projected and re-attended from scratch, giving a T x T score matrix.

363.text: The cached input: exactly one position. This is the asymmetry the whole lab is about — one row of queries against the full history instead of T of them.

364.text: A synthetic cache of the right shape stands in for a real one. What is being timed is the 1 x T attention and the cache concatenation, and neither cares whether the stored keys are meaningful.

368.text: More repetitions at short lengths, fewer at long ones, so every row gets a fair shot at its own minimum without the T = 2048 row dominating the runtime of the whole file.

369.text: One untimed call per path first. The first allocation of a large tensor is slower than every later one, and a warm-up is the difference between measuring attention and measuring the allocator.

371.text: Best-of-N for the naive step: recompute Q, K, V for the whole prefix and run a T x T attention.

372.text: Best-of-N for the cached step: one position's Q, K, V against the cached history, a 1 x T attention. Same module, same weights, same machine — only the shapes differ.

374.text: Print the measured ratio next to the theoretical T. On this box it climbs from under 2x at T = 64 to several hundred times at T = 2048 — the right shape, and comfortably short of theory.

377.text: The curve grows with T because naive attention is T x T against the cache's 1 x T. It stays under the theoretical T because the projections and the fixed per-call overhead do not shrink at all.

381.text: At T = 64 that fixed overhead still swamps everything — which is exactly what the 20-name wall clock above was measuring. Same code, same optimization, two different answers, and the difference is entirely the context length.

404.text: At 2048 context (2T+1)/3 is 1366x fewer attention operations, and the next sentence exists to stop that being read as a 1366x speedup. Projections, MLP, and the memory traffic reading the cache back do not shrink by that factor.

408.text: The end-to-end win is large enough that no serving system ships without the cache, and still smaller than the operation count — bounded by whatever does not get cheaper. Past a few thousand tokens decode is memory-bound rather than compute-bound, so the bound is real, not pedantic.
